precepts.text: He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.
precepts.point: Do we give a physical offering today? No. So what do we offer? We offer ourselves, we offer obedience.

note.label: In Vain Do They Worship Me! Religious Syncretism

precepts.why:
Solomon offered “according to the commandment of Moses”, on the sabbaths, the new moons and the solemn feasts, “three times in the year”: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of weeks and the feast of tabernacles. It is the same law given in Deuteronomy 16:16: “Three times in a year shall all thy males appear before the Lord thy God”, and “they shall not appear before the Lord empty.” So we are supposed to gather and give an offering three times a year. We come together.

But do we give a physical offering today? No. So what do we offer? We offer ourselves; we offer obedience. Sirach puts it plainly: “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.”

Keeping the law is the offering. The one who takes heed to the commandment is not coming before the Lord empty; his obedience is his peace offering. That is how Israel keeps these feasts now, the feast of weeks, which is Pentecost, among them: by gathering together and bringing a life that keeps the commandments.

precepts.text: The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds, and the Lord hears it.
precepts.point: Thou desirest not sacrifice, thou delightest not in burnt offering; the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit and a contrite heart. The animals were temporary; a broken and humbled mind is the sacrifice he wants, and only then are the bullocks on the altar acceptable.

note.label: The Mercy and Humility of King Manasseh

precepts.why:
Psalms 51:17 says “a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” Ecclesiasticus 35:17 shows what happens when the humbled one prays.

“The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds.” It pierces the clouds: the Lord hears it. “And till it come nigh, he will not be comforted; and will not depart, till the most High shall behold to judge righteously, and execute judgment.”

That is David in Psalms 51. When Nathan confronted him after Bathsheba and Uriah, he did not stay the smartest guy in the room. He said, you are right, I am guilty: “For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.” He kept the promise he made in Psalms 32:5, “I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid.” He held himself accountable, and you have to hold yourself accountable when it comes to your sins.

The bones that were broken were his humbling: being confronted with his wrong, confessing it and acknowledging it, and the consequences that followed. And out of that broken, humbled place he prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” That is the prayer of the humble, the one that pierces the clouds, and it is the same humility that brought mercy to King Manasseh.

precepts.text: He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, he that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour, and to depart from wickedness is propitiation.
precepts.point: Whosoever shall keep the whole law and yet offend in one point is guilty of all: the Christian says you cannot keep them, but the context is the royal law, as the next verse shows, he that said do not commit adultery said also do not kill. Speak and do as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty, since Christ redeemed us from the death the moral law carried; he shall have judgment without mercy that hath showed no mercy.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Works Of The Law & Liberty

precepts.why:
Mark 12:33 said loving God and your neighbour is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Ecclesiasticus 35 says the same.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” Keeping the law is offering enough.

“He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour.” Under the offerings, you offered an animal, or fine flour if you were poor. Here, requiting a good turn, which is loving your neighbour as yourself, is the fine flour. “And he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.”

“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” Propitiation means mercy, reconciliation. Departing from wickedness toward your neighbour is what reconciles you to God, which is why the royal law of James 2:8 stands above the sacrifices.

precepts.text: Keeping the law brings offerings enough; that is our offering with no temple standing.
precepts.point: In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
In our captivity there is no Levitical priesthood and no temple, so there is no altar to sprinkle blood upon or lay the parts in order. What is our offering? “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.”

Keeping the commandments is the offering. He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough; that is our offering with no temple standing.

precepts.text: Keeping the law brings offerings enough; the work you put in is your offering, and the Lord extends the more mercy.
precepts.point: Sacrifices are symbolic of your works. The Most High knows how much you can do for this truth, whether you are being slack, slothful, and cheap, or going above and beyond; Abel went above and beyond, and Cain was mediocre. Our sacrifices today are keeping the commandments, the work we put in, the alms we give, and the time we sacrifice.

note.label: Leviticus 2: The Meat Offering of Fine Flour

precepts.why:
“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” The firstfruits and the meat offering were symbolic, and what they stood for is our works.

Keeping the law brings offerings enough. The work you put in is your offering: the commandments kept, the alms given, the time sacrificed. Give it like Abel, above and beyond, not like Cain, and the Lord extends the more mercy.

precepts.text: Keeping the law brings offerings enough; departing from wickedness and forsaking unrighteousness is the propitiation now.
precepts.point: If ye love him, keep his commandments, and he will send the Comforter, the Spirit of truth, which the world cannot receive; the Holy Ghost teaches all things and brings all things to remembrance, and that spirit is how this truth is understood in these last days.

note.label: Numbers 29: The Feasts of the Seventh Month

precepts.why:
Every set feast in Numbers 29 came with its burnt offerings, meat offerings, drink offerings and peace offerings. Ecclesiasticus shows what stands in their place: “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.”

“He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour; and he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.” The fine flour of the meat offering and the sacrifice of praise are now a good turn requited and alms given.

“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” Departing from wickedness and forsaking unrighteousness is the propitiation now. Keeping the law brings offerings enough, so the feasts are kept without the animal sacrifice.

precepts.text: Today's peace offering is keeping the commandments.
precepts.point: The Most High hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land; if you do not want the Lord to have a controversy with you, keep the laws. And keeping the laws is more than beards, fringes, borders of blue, and not eating pork: it is purging the unfruitful spirits you know dwell inside you, the jealousy, envy, covetousness, malice, hatred, grudging, backbiting, murmuring, and gossip.

note.label: Joshua 8: The Taking of Ai and the Blessings and Cursings

precepts.why:
Joshua “offered thereon burnt offerings unto the Lord, and sacrificed peace offerings.” We are still under the law of sacrifice today, but the sacrifice is your body, not the blood of bulls and goats: you sacrifice time, money, pain and labor to push this truth and do the work, spiritual sacrifices through your works by keeping the laws.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” The peace offering today is keeping the commandments. Under grace, peace is a dispensation: the more sin you commit, the less peace you will have. So keep the commandments, and do not frustrate the grace and peace the Most High has with you.

precepts.text: He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering, which was a sacrifice.
precepts.point: Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in the Lord. The sacrifice of righteousness today is keeping the law and presenting your body a living sacrifice.

note.label: Psalm 4: The Lord Hath Set Apart Him That Is Godly for Himself

precepts.why:
“Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in the Lord.” What is the sacrifice of righteousness today? “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” The peace offering was a sacrifice; keeping the law and taking heed to the commandment is offering it. “He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour; and he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.”

So the sacrifice of righteousness today is keeping the law. He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough, and that is how we offer it and put our trust in the Lord.

precepts.text: He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough.
precepts.point: For thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it; thou delightest not in burnt offerings. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David.

note.label: Psalm 51: Acknowledge, Repent, and Be Cleansed

precepts.why: “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” Keeping the law is offerings enough. The Most High does not desire sacrifice or delight in burnt offering; what he wants is the man who keeps his law. That is the offering David knew to bring, and Christ taught nothing different.

precepts.text: He that taketh heed to the Commandments offereth a peace offering.
precepts.point: For thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it; thou delightest not in burnt offerings. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David.

note.label: Psalm 51: Acknowledge, Repent, and Be Cleansed

precepts.why: “He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour; and he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise.” Read with the verse before it: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering, and he that requites a good turn and gives alms is bringing fine flour and a sacrifice of praise. Those are the sacrifices the Most High wants, not the burnt offering David says he delights not in. Obedience and doing good to your brother are the offering.

precepts.text: To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Most High; when you leave sin and repent that is your offering.
precepts.point: For thou desirest not sacrifice, else would I give it; thou delightest not in burnt offerings. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different than David.

note.label: Psalm 51: Acknowledge, Repent, and Be Cleansed

precepts.why:
“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” When you leave sin and repent, that is your offering. Forsaking unrighteousness is the propitiation.

That is why David could say the Most High desires not sacrifice. What pleases him is a man departing from wickedness, which is what David is doing in this whole psalm. Christ left us his example and taught nothing different.

precepts.text: He that serveth the Most High is accepted with favor and his prayer reaches unto the clouds, and the prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds.
precepts.point: The way to get the Most High to hear our prayers is righteousness. His eyes are over the righteous and His ears are open to their prayers, but His face is against them that do evil.

note.label: Psalm 55: Cast Thy Burden Upon the Lord

precepts.why:
“He that serveth the Lord shall be accepted with favour, and his prayer shall reach unto the clouds. The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds: and till it come nigh, he will not be comforted; and will not depart, till the most High shall behold to judge righteously, and execute judgment.” He that serves the Most High is accepted with favour, and his prayer reaches unto the clouds. The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds and will not depart until the most High beholds and executes judgment.

That is David's prayer in Psalm 55, mourning and making a noise because of the voice of the enemy and the oppression of the wicked. His ears are open to the prayers of the righteous, and the prayer of the humble servant does not stop until he judges.

precepts.text: When you keep the law you bring offerings enough; keeping the commandment is the peace offering.
precepts.point: Bring an offering and come into His courts. Do we sacrifice? No, we do not sacrifice anymore, so the offering we bring is keeping the commandments, doing God's commandments.

note.label: Psalm 96: Declare His Glory Among the Heathen

precepts.why:
Bring an offering, and come into his courts. Do we sacrifice? No, we do not sacrifice anymore, so what offering do we bring? “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.”

Keeping the law is offerings enough, and taking heed to the commandment is the peace offering. The offering we bring into his courts today is doing God's commandments. That is how we give unto the Lord the glory due unto his name, the honour for what he has done for Israel: he put us in slavery, and now he is bringing us back to his glory, our glory, where we once were as a people.

points: Propitiation goes back to atonement or reconciliation to the Lord, bringing you close to the Lord.

In all thy gifts shew a cheerful countenance: that spirit is contagious. Some of y'all walk around with a miserable countenance, sad all the time, looking up here on purpose for attention. We ignore that.

Do not think to corrupt with gifts: you can't have a hatred for your brother but offer the best sacrifice and think the Most High will overlook it. I'll offer the best of my flock, but I can't stand that brother across the street? That is a corrupt gift. If you got hatred for your brother, it's a waste of sacrifice.
